## Today in One Minute

- A beginner-friendly Python tutorial shows how to build a simple AI agent step by step, lowering the entry bar for diploma students.
- Google Chromebooks have added a Face Control accessibility feature powered by Gemini, letting students operate a laptop using head movements and facial gestures.
- NVIDIA Nemotron-Labs released a diffusion-based language model that aims to generate text much faster than traditional token-by-token models.

## What Happened

- Towards Data Science published a beginner's guide to building an AI agent in Python, walking through the core idea of an agent that can reason, call tools, and complete tasks.
- Google introduced Face Control on Chromebooks, an accessibility feature using on-device AI and Gemini to let users move the cursor and click using their face and head, aimed at students with limited mobility.
- NVIDIA's Hugging Face post describes Nemotron-Labs diffusion language models, which generate text in parallel rather than one token at a time, promising big speed improvements for text generation.

## Why It Matters

- A clear Python agent tutorial gives IT and AI lecturers a ready-made teaching path for introducing agents to diploma students without needing heavy frameworks or paid tools.
- Face Control on Chromebooks is a concrete example of AI for inclusion that lecturers can show students, making accessibility tangible rather than abstract and supporting RP's diverse learner needs.
- Faster generation through diffusion language models matters because it changes what is feasible in classroom demos and student projects, such as real-time tutoring or interactive lab assistants, and gives a fresh case for discussing how language models actually work.

## Try This Today

- Spend 15 minutes following the Towards Data Science agent tutorial on your Windows 11 laptop in VS Code, then note one section that diploma students would find confusing so you can pre-empt it in class.
- Watch the Chromebook Face Control demo and list two RP courses or scenarios where this accessibility feature could be discussed, for example in UX, healthcare informatics, or inclusive design modules.
- Skim the Nemotron-Labs diffusion language model post and write a one-paragraph plain-English explanation of "diffusion vs token-by-token generation" you could share with a class.

## Teaching Angle

- Run a short lab where students follow the Python agent tutorial, then ask each pair to add one new tool (for example, a calculator or file reader) and demo it. Good for a 1 to 2 hour applied AI session.
- Use Face Control as a quick discussion prompt: ask students to brainstorm three other AI accessibility ideas, and one risk or limitation for each. Fits naturally in ethics, HCI, or design thinking lessons.
- For a foundational AI module, set a compare-and-contrast task: students draw a simple diagram showing how a normal language model generates text versus how a diffusion language model does it, based on the Nemotron-Labs article.

## Links

- [The Ultimate Beginners' Guide to Building an AI Agent in Python](https://towardsdatascience.com/the-ultimate-beginners-guide-to-building-an-ai-agent-in-python/)
- [Here's how accessibility tools and Gemini are helping students find independence](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/chromebooks/face-control/)
- [Towards Speed-of-Light Text Generation with Nemotron-Labs Diffusion Language Models](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/nemotron-labs-diffusion)
